title: Tomorrow
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Spanish has three ways of talking about tomorrow, and the one-word -ré future is the one people reach for least. The everyday future is voy a + the plain verb — Mañana voy a trabajar. The plain present does the job too once a time word is there (Mañana trabajo). trabajaré is real Spanish, but it belongs to writing, to promises and to predictions rather than to what you are doing after breakfast.

The a in voy a trabajar is obligatory and means nothing on its own — it is the glue between the going and the doing. English hides it inside "going to", so the commonest slip is to leave it out: *Voy trabajar is not a sentence.
ir ("to go") keeps almost nothing of itself when it conjugates: voy · vas · va · vamos · van. There is no stem to learn — the five shapes are learned whole, the way hice and fui were in M5.

After voy a the second verb never takes an ending: Voy a comer, never *Voy a como. Only the ir half moves for the person — voy a comer, vas a comer, vamos a comer — and the plain infinitive sits there unchanged.

What follows the a decides what voy a is saying. A plain verb makes it a plan: Voy a trabajar, "I'm going to work". A place makes it real movement: Voy a México, "I'm going to Mexico". The same two words do both jobs, exactly as M5's fui did for ir and ser.

The plain present is already a future once a time word says so: Mañana trabajo is "I work tomorrow". English does this too, so nothing new has to be learned — the only difference is that Spanish needs no "am" and no "-ing" to do it.

The one-word future is built on the WHOLE infinitive plus an ending: trabajar + é = trabajaré, hablar + é = hablaré. Nothing is cut off first, which is why the r is still in there — and it is what keeps M5's hablé (I spoke) apart from hablaré (I will speak).

mañana does two jobs and the words around it choose: alone it is "tomorrow" (Mañana trabajo), and inside por la mañana it is the morning (Trabajo por la mañana). One sentence can hold both — Mañana trabajo por la mañana. English has two separate words here and Spanish has one.
no goes in front of the going, not in front of the doing: Mañana no voy a trabajar. *Voy a no trabajar hangs the negative on the wrong verb, which is not how the plan is refused.
vamos a + a plain verb is two things at once: "we are going to …" and "let's …". Vamos a comer is a plan or an invitation, and only the situation tells them apart.
A day of the week takes el and no word for "on": El sábado voy a México — literally "the Saturday". Make it plural and it becomes a habit: los sábados is "on Saturdays".

words.note: On its own it is "tomorrow". The same word inside M4's por la mañana is the morning — one word, two jobs, and the phrase around it decides which. It usually opens the sentence, the way Ayer does.
ir ("to go") in the "I" form. Nothing of the infinitive survives in it, and it is the engine of the whole module: voy a + a plain verb is how a plan is said.
The dictionary form of the verb behind M4's trabajo and M5's trabajé. After voy a it stays exactly like this — the person is already carried by voy.

sentences.trap: English says "going to work" and hears one word where Spanish writes two: voy and a. The a carries no meaning and cannot be dropped.
sentences.sound: ma-ÑA-na. The ñ is the ny of "canyon", and the stress sits in the middle. voy rhymes with English "boy", with a v that is softer than an English one.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to study
variations.changed: swap the plain verb — the frame never moves

variations.display: Voy a trabajar por la mañana
variations.cue: I'm going to work in the morning
variations.changed: the other mañana, back inside its three-word phrase

mistake.why: The a is not optional. voy a trabajar — the going, the a, then the doing.

sentences.usage: The plainest way to say what tomorrow holds.
sentences.mnemonic: voy · a · the plain verb. Three pieces, always three.

sentences.cue: Are you going to eat with Ana?

words.note: ir for tú. voy and vas are the same verb and share no letters with it: voy · vas · va · vamos · van. As ever, no tú in front — vas already says who.

sentences.trap: English needs three words to ask this — "are you going" — and Spanish needs one. The question is the statement with the two marks around it; nothing moves.
sentences.sound: One syllable, BAS, with the s clear at the end. Spanish has no buzzing z sound here.

variations.cue: Are you going to eat with Rohan?
variations.changed: swap who you are eating with

variations.cue: Are you going to work tomorrow?
variations.changed: another plan, same question shape

mistake.why: Drop the tú. vas already names the person, and putting it back sounds like you are picking that person out from someone else.

sentences.mnemonic: voy for me, vas for you — one letter's worth of family resemblance.

words.note: "Later on", with no clock attached — it points at a time after now rather than at an hour. It sits at the end of the sentence, where English also puts "later".

sentences.trap: A plan does not need a day on it. voy a + a plain verb covers anything from five minutes away to next year; después just says "after this".
sentences.sound: des-PUÉS. The accent puts the stress on the last syllable and keeps the u and the e running together as one glide.

variations.cue: Later I'm going to study
variations.changed: the time word moves to the front — both orders are normal

variations.cue: I'm going to eat later
variations.changed: swap the plain verb

mistake.why: estudio is "I study". After voy a the verb keeps its dictionary shape: voy a estudiar.

sentences.usage: Putting something off without naming a time.
sentences.mnemonic: después = after this — and it comes after the verb.

sentences.display: Mañana no voy a hacer nada
sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'm not going to do anything
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Tomorrow not I-go to do nothing" — both negatives stay
sentences.literal: Tomorrow not I-go to to-do nothing

words.note: The dictionary form of M5's hice and hiciste. One verb for both English words: hacer la comida is making it, hacer el trabajo is doing it.

sentences.trap: The negative goes on the going: no voy a hacer. English can say "I'm going to do nothing", and Spanish still puts no in front of the verb and keeps nada as well.
sentences.sound: a-CER. The h is silent, as it always is, and the c before an e is an s across Latin America and a th in most of Spain.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to do a lot
variations.changed: the opposite plan, with M1's mucho

variations.cue: What are you going to do tomorrow?
variations.changed: the question this sentence answers

mistake.display: Mañana voy a no hacer nada
mistake.why: no belongs in front of voy, not in front of hacer: Mañana no voy a hacer nada.

sentences.mnemonic: hice yesterday, hacer tomorrow — same verb, two ends of the week.

sentences.cue: Are you going to study tonight?

words.note: Two words where English has one: "this night". It is a different thing from M4's por la noche, which is "at night" in general — esta noche is the one that is coming.

sentences.trap: esta noche is a plan, por la noche is a habit. Trabajo por la noche says what your nights are usually like; Voy a trabajar esta noche says what tonight holds.
sentences.sound: ES-ta NO-che. The ch is the ch of English "church", and neither word carries an accent because both are stressed where Spanish expects.

variations.cue: Tonight I'm going to study
variations.changed: the answer, with the time word in front

variations.cue: Are you going to eat tonight?
variations.changed: swap the plain verb

mistake.why: That asks about your nights in general. For the night ahead, say esta noche.

sentences.usage: Making a plan for the evening.
sentences.mnemonic: esta noche is THIS night; por la noche is any night.

words.note: Three words that travel as one, and one letter apart from M4's todos los días: todo el día is a single day from end to end, todos los días is every day of the week. Singular for the stretch, plural for the habit.

sentences.trap: M4's trabajo has not changed at all; the future is coming entirely from mañana. Take the time word away and the same sentence is about today.
sentences.sound: TO-do el DÍ-a, run together into three beats. día carries its accent to split the i from the a and keep the stress on it.

variations.cue: Tomorrow I work in the morning
variations.changed: both jobs of mañana in one sentence

variations.cue: I work every day
variations.changed: the plural — a habit rather than one long day

mistake.why: todos los días is every day, so it cannot be pinned to tomorrow. One day from end to end is todo el día.

sentences.usage: Warning someone you will be busy.
sentences.mnemonic: todo el día — one day, whole. todos los días — all the days.

words.note: The one-word future: the whole infinitive hablar with -é stuck on the end. That is why the r is still there, and it is the only thing keeping it apart from M5's hablé (I spoke). Spoken Spanish would more often say voy a hablar; this form leans towards a promise or a prediction.

sentences.trap: hablé and hablaré are one syllable apart and two tenses apart — one is yesterday, the other is tomorrow. The r is the whole difference, and it is the r of the infinitive.
sentences.sound: a-bla-RÉ, three syllables with the stress on the last. Beside M5's a-BLÉ, which has two.

variations.display: Mañana voy a hablar con Ana
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to speak with Ana
variations.changed: the everyday way of saying the same plan

variations.cue: Tomorrow I'll work a lot
variations.changed: the same ending on another -ar verb

mistake.why: hablé is the past. Tomorrow needs the r of the infinitive underneath the ending: hablaré.

sentences.usage: A promise rather than a plan.
sentences.mnemonic: Keep the whole infinitive, then add the ending: hablar + é.

sentences.display: Vamos a comer a las ocho
sentences.cue: We're going to eat at eight
sentences.glossEn: lit. "We-go to eat at the eight"
sentences.literal: We-go to to-eat at the eight

words.note: ir for "we", and the only shape of it that also works as an invitation: Vamos a comer is both "we are going to eat" and "let's eat". English keeps those two apart with different words; Spanish leaves it to the moment.

sentences.trap: Both a's in this sentence are M4's one-letter signpost, in two of its seats: the first glues the plan together, the second points at a clock time.
sentences.sound: VA-mos, stressed on the first syllable — not va-MOS.

variations.cue: Let's study tonight
variations.changed: read as an invitation rather than a plan

variations.cue: We're going to eat early
variations.changed: M4's temprano instead of an hour

mistake.why: The plan a is missing. vamos a comer, exactly as voy a comer.

sentences.mnemonic: Vamos a … is half plan, half invitation.

sentences.cue: On Saturday I'm going to Mexico
sentences.glossEn: lit. "The Saturday I-go to Mexico" — no word for "on"

words.note: Saturday, masculine and written with a small s — the days of the week are not capitalised in Spanish. el sábado is "on Saturday"; los sábados is "on Saturdays", every week. The accent marks the stress on the first of its three syllables.

sentences.trap: Here voy a is not a plan at all — a place after the a makes it real movement. Voy a trabajar is what I will do; Voy a México is where I am going.
sentences.sound: SÁ-ba-do. Three syllables, the first one loudest, and the b in the middle is soft — nearer an English v than a b.

variations.cue: On Saturday I'm going to India
variations.changed: swap the destination

variations.cue: On Saturdays I don't work
variations.changed: the plural turns one day into every week

mistake.why: Spanish has no word for "on" with a day. The article does it: el sábado.

sentences.mnemonic: el sábado — the article is the "on".

sentences.display: Mañana voy a ver una película
sentences.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to see a film
sentences.glossEn: lit. "Tomorrow I-go to see a film"
sentences.literal: Tomorrow I-go to to-see a film

words.note: The dictionary form of M4's veo. It covers watching as well as seeing — ver una película is what English calls watching a film.

sentences.trap: No personal a here. M4's a in front of a person marks a person; a film is a thing, so nothing stands in front of it — the only a in this sentence is the plan a after voy.
sentences.sound: One syllable, BER, and the r at the end is one light tap of the tongue.

variations.display: Mañana voy a ver a mi hermana
variations.cue: Tomorrow I'm going to see my sister
variations.changed: a person, so M4's personal a comes back — two a's in a row

variations.display: Esta noche voy a ver una película
variations.cue: Tonight I'm going to see a film
variations.changed: swap the time word

mistake.why: The plan needs its a: voy a ver.

sentences.usage: The evening plan almost everyone has.
sentences.mnemonic: veo today, voy a ver tomorrow.
